clue.text: Amount drunk at the table where the men are

parts.note: a draught is a single swallow or measure of drink taken in one go
a board is an old word for a table, as in bed and board

explanation.surface: A drinker downs a measure at the table where the menfolk are sitting.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'men' are the pieces in the game of draughts (checkers in the US), so the place where they stand is the playing surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Draughtsmen are the playing pieces of checkers, and they sit on the chequered playing surface.

clue.text: Harangue medical assembly

indicators.note: an assembly is something put together from parts, so the letters of medical are put together afresh

explanation.surface: A doctor rants at a gathering of the medical profession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'assembly' looks like a meeting of doctors, but it signals that the letters of MEDICAL are assembled into a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: To harangue is to make a loud, forceful speech, which is what declaiming means.

clue.text: Own up, and get a mark over it

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece over another means it is written above it

parts.note: DM is the abbreviation for the Deutschmark, the old German currency
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is told to confess and accept a black mark for the offence.
explanation.walkthrough: The mark is the Deutschmark, Germany's currency before the euro, abbreviated DM, not a blemish or a grade.
explanation.definitionFit: To own up is to confess, which is to admit a fault.

clue.text: Oliver or Winston in 19847

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held 'Oliver or Winston in 19847' is OCR-garbled ('19847'); Oliver Goldsmith fits, but nothing in the held text accounts for GOLD in a Winston (Smith, of 1984) reading, and the scan does not show the clues.

clue.text: Parasite not unknown in amphibian creature

indicators.note: not means the following letter is left out of the word before it

parts.note: a toady is a sycophant who lives off flattering others, a human parasite
Y is one of the letters used in algebra for an unknown quantity

explanation.surface: A biologist finds no unknown parasite living inside an amphibian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not unknown' reads as a double negative, but it tells you to drop Y, an algebraic unknown, from TOADY.
explanation.definitionFit: The toad is a familiar tailless amphibian, close kin to the frog.

clue.text: Exits — following the Great?

definitions.meaning: doors leading out of a building
the phrase the Great ..., meaning open country, completes it

explanation.surface: Ways out lead to the great open country beyond.
explanation.definitionFit: Exits are doors that take you out, and the Great Outdoors is the stock phrase for wild open nature.

clue.text: Shakespearean princess whose sister was poisonous to her

definitions.text: Shakespearean princess whose sister was poisonous to her

parts.words: Shakespearean princess whose sister was poisonous to her
parts.note: in King Lear one of the king's daughters is poisoned by her elder sister Goneril

explanation.surface: A Shakespeare heroine is done in by a venomous sibling.
explanation.walkthrough: In King Lear, Goneril poisons her sister out of jealousy over Edmund; 'poisonous' is literal, not just spiteful.
explanation.definitionFit: She is Lear's second daughter, whom Goneril kills with poison in the play's last act.

clue.text: Women kidnapped by seaman in heinous crime? I expect something will turn up!

definitions.text: I expect something will turn up!

indicators.note: in places the seaman-and-women piece inside the scrambled letters
a heinous crime is a wicked distortion, so the letters of crime are distorted into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder

indicators.note: being kidnapped means being held inside the captor, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: AB stands for able seaman, a rating in the Royal Navy

explanation.surface: A sailor abducts some women in a wicked crime, hoping his luck will change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kidnapped by' holds the women inside the seaman, and 'in' sets that inside the letters of 'crime' reordered by 'heinous'. The definition is the catchphrase of the ever-hopeful debtor in Dickens's David Copperfield.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's optimistic debtor is forever saying he is waiting for something to turn up, so the catchphrase identifies him.

clue.text: Communications session run by media

parts.note: media is read as the plural of medium, a spiritualist who passes on messages from the dead

explanation.surface: It looks like a broadcasting or press briefing organised by journalists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'media' suggests newspapers and broadcasters, but here it is the plural of 'medium', a spiritualist.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiritualists hold sittings at which a medium claims to relay messages from the departed.

clue.text: Feeling obliged to change direction of road in grievance

indicators.note: changing direction means turning the road's letters round where they sit

parts.note: a complaint is a grievance someone voices
the A1 is Britain's longest numbered road, written AI in crosswords

explanation.surface: A motorist, forced to divert a road, feels aggrieved.
explanation.walkthrough: The road is the A1, Britain's great north road, with its 1 read as the letter I; 'change direction of' turns those two letters round where they stand in the grievance.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone compliant goes along with what is asked, feeling bound to obey.

clue.text: One conducting good Scots to the capital in Edinburgh

parts.note: guid is the Scots spelling of good

indicators.note: the capital of a word is its first letter, its capital letter

explanation.surface: A tour leader takes good Scottish folk to the city sights of Edinburgh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'capital' tempts you to think of Edinburgh as Scotland's capital; it means its capital letter, E.
explanation.definitionFit: A guide leads visitors round, conducting a party through a place.

clue.text: Demonstrate during international cricket

parts.note: at can mean during, as in at night
a Test is a full international cricket match between countries

explanation.surface: Protesters demonstrate while a Test match is being played.
explanation.walkthrough: A Test match is an international cricket fixture, often lasting five days.
explanation.definitionFit: To attest is to bear witness, to show or prove something true.

clue.text: Denton's faction fashioned from 18ac by exaggerator

definitions.meaning: the radical Jacobin group in the French Revolution's Convention to which Danton belonged sat on the high benches
the idiom about making a big fuss out of a little thing turns the 18 across into something huge

explanation.surface: A political party is made out of a trifle by someone who overstates things.
explanation.walkthrough: The faction is the Montagnards of the French Revolution, named for their high seats; the second reading uses the idiom 'make a mountain out of a molehill'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Montagnards were known in English by their nickname, and exaggerators proverbially turn a molehill into a peak.

clue.text: There's a mess at home, so share the chores

parts.note: muck is dirt or a mess
in means at home, as in staying in

explanation.surface: With the house in a state, everyone must pitch in with the housework.
explanation.definitionFit: To muck in is the British idiom for pitching in and doing your share of the work.

clue.text: Speed — it's injected into salad plant

indicators.note: injected means pushed inside, so one piece goes into the other

parts.note: celery is a crunchy vegetable eaten raw in salads
it is read as the word it

explanation.surface: Something is quickly injected into a salad vegetable.
explanation.definitionFit: Celerity is a formal word for swiftness or rapid motion.

clue.text: Odds-on Gilbert being taken*" in by The Common Man

indicators.note: being taken in means held inside, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a prole is a member of the working masses, from Orwell's 1984
Bab was the pen name of W. S. Gilbert, used for his comic verse the Bab Ballads

explanation.surface: A favourite writer is fooled by an ordinary fellow.
explanation.walkthrough: Gilbert, of Gilbert and Sullivan, signed his early comic poems Bab; prole, a working-class person, comes from Orwell's 1984.
explanation.definitionFit: An odds-on outcome is one more likely than not, the bookmakers' term for a likely winner.

clue.text: Highwayman, too, wears a short jacket

indicators.note: the jacket wears the other piece, wrapping round it like clothing

parts.note: a bolero is a short open jacket ending above the waist
and means also or too

explanation.surface: A robber of the road also sports a little jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wears' reads as the highwayman dressing, but it is the jacket that wraps round AND.
explanation.definitionFit: A bandolero is a Spanish bandit or brigand who robs travellers on the road.

clue.text: Biscuit to be stirred up? You'll need a white bowl

parts.note: to flap is to get agitated or flustered
in the game of bowls the jack is the small white target ball

explanation.surface: Someone baking a biscuit to be mixed up is told to fetch a white bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: In lawn bowls, a British green game, the jack is the small white ball players aim at; 'bowl' is not a mixing bowl.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a flapjack is a chewy oat bar or biscuit made with syrup and butter.

clue.text: The entire factory, Spooner tells us, is put up by 4s friend

indicators.note: Spooner's slips swap the opening sounds of two words, so the two spoken words exchange starts

parts.note: the whole means the entire thing
a mill is a factory, such as a cotton mill

explanation.surface: The whole factory is apparently built by a friend of the 4.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the opening sounds of 'whole mill' to hear MOLE HILL. 4 down is Toad, and in The Wind in the Willows Toad's friend is Mole, who throws up a little heap of earth.
explanation.definitionFit: A mole digging tunnels pushes up a small heap of soil, the thing it builds above ground.

clue.text: He's composed from Harlem

indicators.note: from here means the letters are made out of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A man stays calm when he comes from a New York neighbourhood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composed' reads as calm, but the definition means a man who composed music; 'from' shows the letters are rearranged out of HARLEM.
explanation.definitionFit: Gustav Mahler was an Austrian composer of grand symphonies.

clue.text: Doubtless her picture is in a metal frame

parts.note: taken as written
a grid is a framework of metal bars

explanation.surface: A woman's photograph is certainly framed in metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'her' stands for a woman's name: her picture is IN a GRID, and the clue hints at the film star Ingrid Bergman, whose pictures were films.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun stands for a woman bearing this Scandinavian name, such as the actress Bergman.

clue.text: Venus and Adonis's first two characters meet drunken satyr

indicators.note: drunken means reeling about, so the letters are thrown into a new order
the first two characters of the name are its opening pair of letters

explanation.surface: The goddess and her young lover meet a tipsy woodland creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunken' turns AD (the opening two letters of Adonis) plus SATYR into a new order. 'Venus and Adonis' looks like Shakespeare's poem, but Venus alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Venus shining at dawn is called the morning star, an old name for which is this compound.

clue.text: Dance for the Navy during Indian training exercises

indicators.note: during means within, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: the Hopi are a Native American people of Arizona
RN stands for the Royal Navy
PE is physical education, school exercise classes

explanation.surface: A naval dance is staged during exercises by an Indian unit.
explanation.walkthrough: The Indian is a Native American Hopi, not someone from India; PE is physical education, the school gym lesson.
explanation.definitionFit: The hornpipe is a lively solo dance traditionally associated with sailors.

clue.text: Write to church for money

parts.note: to pen is to write
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Someone writes to the church asking for funds.
explanation.definitionFit: Pence are small British coins, a form of cash.

clue.text: City that's explosive indeed

parts.note: a bomb is an explosive device
ay is an old form of yes, used like indeed

explanation.surface: A city is described as truly explosive.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the name of India's great western port city, now Mumbai.

clue.text: Mark's drink is nearly finished

indicators.note: nearly finished means the word stops just short of its last letter

parts.note: brandy is a spirit distilled from wine

explanation.surface: Mark's glass of spirits is almost empty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' looks like a man's name owning the drink, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A brand is a mark burned into an animal's hide, or a trademark.

clue.text: Bridge team

definitions.meaning: to bridge something is to stretch across it
a pair of horses or oxen harnessed together

explanation.definitionFit: A bridge stretches across a gap as an arch does, and a matched pair of draught animals is called this.

clue.text: Dramatic vehicle for Covent Garden?

parts.note: names a Shaw play title that is also a fruit barrow suited to the old London fruit and vegetable market

explanation.surface: It asks which theatrical showpiece suits the Royal Opera House district.
explanation.walkthrough: Covent Garden suggests the opera house, but it was also London's fruit and vegetable market; The Apple Cart is a play by George Bernard Shaw.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaw's political comedy shares its name with the barrow a fruit seller pushes through a market.

clue.text: Exemplified by "Kiss me, hardy?.

parts.note: Nelson's dying words to Captain Hardy are read as a command to give a kiss

explanation.surface: Nelson's famous last words at Trafalgar are offered as an example of something.
explanation.walkthrough: A peck is a quick kiss, so Nelson's request is literally an order for a peck; the phrase really means a social hierarchy.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means a ranking of who dominates whom, first seen in hens pecking each other.
